newsitem.title: INDIA: India crash highlights flight from economic woes.
newsitem.headline: India crash highlights flight from economic woes.

text.p: The mangled wreckage of the two aircraft that collided near Delhi tell a poignant story of Kazakh businessmen and Asian workers, both flying abroad to escape their countries' economic woes.

Most of the passengers aboard the Saudi Arabian jumbo which collided with a Kazakh freighter were workers from India and Nepal, heading for the Saudi city of Dharan, one of many Gulf centres that attract skilled and unskilled Asians.
The KazAir Ilyushin Il-76 freighter was carrying 27 businessmen and 10 other people on a chartered flight, one of scores carrying traders that land in Delhi from Central Asian countries every month.
The two planes crashed near the Indian capital shortly after a mid-air collision on Tuesday, killing all 349 people on board.

Daya Ram Mandal's Nepali passport lay covered in a thin film of dust, a few yards from the broken tail of the Saudi plane in a mustard field near the town of Charkhi Dadri, 80 km (50 miles) west of Delhi.
Mandal had changed his profession in the passport from farmer to tailor two months after it was issued in July.
Changing profession is common among Asian workers to get the right working visa in Gulf states.
There was no one from Nepal at the Charkhi Dadri hospital on Wednesday to identify Mandal's body among the steady flow of corpses arriving there from the crash site, six km (four miles) away.
Nepal's Foreign Ministry said 53 people from one of the world's 10 poorest countries were among the 312 aboard the Saudi flight to Dharan and Jeddah.

Achyut Shrestha of Air Express Private Ltd, general sales agent for the Saudi airline in the Himalayan kingdom, said the passengers included 39 workers booked by Gulf Manpower Services, a firm that sends Nepali labourers to Saudi Arabia.
Relatives of some of the 215 Indians aboard wept bitterly over the loss of their families' only bread winners.
Mohammed Sharif Hashmi was a driver in Saudi Arabia.
"He was the eldest in the family and he used to take care of many of our needs and hold us together," Hashmi's brother Mohammad Ali told Reuters, his voice choked with grief. "Now he is gone."

Mohammed Shakil and Parvez Shah were travelling for their first jobs in wealthy Saudi Arabia. They had paid job agents between 20,000 and 30,000 rupees ($570 and $860), a huge amount in India, to get employment visas, relatives said.
"We had hoped he would earn and send back more money," said Imamumddin (one name), Shah's relative from the economically backward state of Bihar. "We are so poor. Now we don't know."

The wreckage revealed an assortment of old clothes, some of them stuffed in sacks. There were letters to relatives. Wedding and other family pictures strewn around the wreckage told a story of long intervals of separation.
Remittances from workers abroad are vital to India's foreign exchange reserves. Their large-scale exodus during the 1991 Gulf war triggered a serious balance of payments crisis for India.
The victims on the Kazhakh plane were traders.
"We know that the businessmen were carrying at least $1.5 million," said Rajiv Bhaskar, an Indian official of KazAir.
"We run about three such flights a week," he told Reuters in the village of Bhiror where the Ilyushin crashed.
The passengers were all familiar travellers to India where the would buy mainly leather and woollen goods, Bhaskar said.

After the fall of the Soviet Union many such traders from poor Central Asian republics embarked on lucrative business in India, buying goods here to sell them at between four and 10 times the price back home.
In May this year, Kazakhstan increased the limit on dollars that individuals are allowed to take out to $10,000 from $500.
Indian officials say many Central Asian women, including Russians, have even embarked on a career in prostitution in India to pay for goods they can sell for a profit at home.
